notes.meaning: As the early church grew, a disagreement arose between Greek-speaking Jewish believers and local Hebrew-speaking believers. The Greek-speaking group felt that their widows were not receiving their fair share of the daily food distribution. This problem came from rapid growth and organizational strain rather than intentional cruelty.

The twelve apostles gathered all the believers together to solve the complaint. They explained that their main calling was to preach God's message, not to manage food supplies and money. They wanted to make sure that essential Bible teaching was not neglected for daily administrative tasks.

The apostles told the congregation to choose seven trustworthy men from among themselves. These men had to show practical wisdom and be visibly guided by the Holy Spirit. The apostles promised to hand over the responsibility of the food program to these qualified leaders.

The apostles stated that they would dedicate their own time to prayer and teaching God's message. Faithful preaching requires deep prayer and complete reliance on God to change lives. Church leaders serve best when they protect their primary spiritual duties from everyday distractions.

The whole church welcomed this wise solution and selected seven men, including Stephen and Philip. All seven had Greek names, showing that the church generously chose leaders from the very group that felt left out. One of them, Nicolas, was an outsider who had embraced Judaism before becoming a follower of Jesus.

differ.view: Reformed churches see this event as the official biblical creation of the office of deacon to care for the poor and manage church funds.
Some evangelicals believe these men were pastoral leaders similar to elders rather than deacons, because they preached and evangelized.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Catholic and Orthodox teaching traces the holy order of the diaconate back to this event, honoring Stephen as the first deacon.

notes.meaning: The believers presented these seven men to the apostles, who prayed and placed their hands on them. This public ceremony officially appointed them to their new role and asked God to bless their work.

differ.view: Some evangelicals hold that laying on hands was only a symbolic ceremony of blessing and commissioning that gave no supernatural power.

notes.meaning: Once this dispute was peacefully resolved, the message of the gospel spread even more widely. The number of disciples in Jerusalem multiplied rapidly, and many Jewish temple priests believed in Jesus. God turned a potential division inside the church into a time of great spiritual growth.

Stephen was filled with God's special grace and spiritual strength. In addition to serving the poor, he began performing amazing signs and miracles among the people. His life proved that God uses dedicated servants for far more than ordinary daily chores.

Trouble soon started when men from a synagogue of freed Roman slaves stood up against Stephen. They were joined by foreign Jews from northern Africa and modern-day Turkey. These men challenged Stephen and began to argue fiercely against his message.

Stephen's opponents could not stand up against his deep wisdom or the Holy Spirit who guided his words. God gave him clear answers from the Scriptures that silenced their objections. The power of divine truth completely defeated their human arguments.

Because they could not win the debate fairly, Stephen's enemies secretly paid men to tell lies about him. These bribed witnesses accused Stephen of speaking insults against Moses and against God. In the Jewish community, such an accusation of blasphemy was a serious charge carrying the death penalty.

The plotters stirred up the crowds, the religious teachers, and the city elders against Stephen. They launched a surprise attack, grabbed him by force, and dragged him before the Sanhedrin, which was the highest Jewish court. Stephen now faced the exact same governing council that had condemned Jesus.

The enemies brought in false witnesses before the high court to testify against Stephen. These witnesses declared that he never stopped speaking against the holy temple and the law of Moses. They took Stephen's genuine words and twisted them into an attack against Jewish sacred beliefs.

The witnesses told the court that Stephen claimed Jesus of Nazareth would destroy the temple and overturn their sacred customs. Stephen had indeed taught that Jesus fulfills the old rituals, but his accusers twisted this to mean he wanted to destroy their faith. Their misleading charges sounded very much like the false claims once made against Jesus at His trial.

All the council members stared directly at Stephen and noticed that his face looked like the face of an angel. God gave him a calm, supernatural brightness that showed his absolute peace and innocence. Just as Moses had a glowing face when he stood before God, Stephen's radiant face proved that God was with him.
